titre: The Aral Sea, Gone for a Cotton Harvest
accroche: In 1960, it was the fourth-largest lake in the world. In 2014, its eastern lobe dried up completely: the result of a decision, not a whim of the climate.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1960, the Aral Sea covered about 68,000 km² on the border between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan: the fourth-largest lake in the world. In 2014, its eastern lobe, east of its southern half, dried up entirely, leaving a desert since named the Aralkum. Between those two dates, no earthquake, no exceptional drought: an administrative decision.

## The Mechanism

The Aral Sea is a closed lake, with no outlet to the ocean: it exists only because two rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, bring it enough water to make up for what the sun makes it lose to evaporation. In the early 1960s, the USSR set out to divert these two rivers into a network of irrigation canals, to turn the arid plains of Central Asia into cotton fields: a crop the Soviet plan wanted to export in bulk. As early as 1960, between 20 and 60 km³ of water a year was already being drawn off before it reached the lake.

Deprived of its inflow, the sea lost about 20 centimeters of level a year between 1961 and 1970, a rate that nearly tripled in the following decade. By 2004, its surface area had fallen to 17,160 km², a quarter of what it was in 1960; between 1960 and 1998, its volume had dropped by 80%. Its salinity, meanwhile, rose from about 10 to 30 grams per liter: close to that of seawater. In 1988, Uzbekistan had become the world's leading cotton exporter.

## The Shift

The story does not end with a verdict of irreversible failure. In 2005, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral Dam, a 13 km dike that separates the small North Aral Sea, closer to the mountains, from the large South Sea, already doomed. Isolated and held back, the North Sea rose by 12 meters between 2003 and 2008; fishing has resumed there, with the return of freshwater species.

In the south, in Uzbekistan, nothing comparable: the sea remains largely dry, and the country continues to bet on cotton irrigation and on oil exploration in the exposed seabed rather than on restoration. The contrast between the two shores tells the same story in reverse: if a single dam was enough to bring one half of the lake back, then the drying of the other half was not a climatic fatality, but the continuation of a choice.

repere.texte: Between 1960 and 1998, the volume of the Aral Sea dropped by 80% and its surface area by 60%; in 2014, the eastern lobe of its southern half disappeared completely, becoming the Aralkum desert.

carte.punch: The fourth-largest lake in the world vanished so that cotton could grow in the desert.
carte.idee: In the 1960s, the USSR diverted the two rivers that fed the Aral Sea to irrigate cotton fields. With no inflow of water, the lake lost 80% of its volume between 1960 and 1998, and its eastern lobe disappeared completely in 2014.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details the full chronology of the drying, the salinity figures, and the Kok-Aral Dam.

quiz.question: Why did the Aral Sea dry up so fast starting in the 1960s?
choix: Because an earthquake opened a fault that drained the lake into the Caspian Sea
Because the climate of Central Asia suddenly warmed, speeding up evaporation
Because the USSR diverted the two rivers that fed it to irrigate cotton fields
Because building the Kok-Aral Dam blocked most of the incoming flow
quiz.explication: The Aral Sea is a lake with no outlet, which exists only because the water brought by the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya makes up for evaporation. Diverted starting in the 1960s to irrigate cotton, these two rivers stopped feeding the lake at the same level, causing it to dry up: the Kok-Aral Dam, built in 2005, did the opposite and let the North Sea rise again.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which dam let the North Aral Sea rise by 12 meters between 2003 and 2008, and who built it?
choix: The Kok-Aral Dam, completed by Kazakhstan in 2005
The Amu Darya Dam, completed by Uzbekistan in 1998
The Syr Darya Dam, built by the USSR in 1965
The Aralkum Dam, funded by the United Nations in 2010
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral Dam in 2005, a 13 km dike that separates the North Aral Sea from the South Sea, letting the former rise by 12 meters in five years.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened in 1988, in connection with the cotton irrigation diverting the waters of the Aral Sea?
choix: The sea's eastern lobe dried up completely for the first time
The USSR halted the diversion of the two rivers to cotton
Uzbekistan became the world's leading cotton exporter
The lake's salinity reached the exact level of seawater
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places in 1988 the moment Uzbekistan becomes the world's leading cotton exporter, a direct result of irrigation fed by the diverted waters of the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is Uzbekistan doing today in the dried-up bed of the South Aral Sea, rather than trying to restore it?
choix: It has turned the area into a strictly protected nature reserve
It is building a second dam twin to the Kok-Aral
It has abandoned agriculture entirely across the whole region
It continues cotton irrigation and explores the subsurface for oil
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Uzbekistan continues to bet on cotton irrigation and on oil exploration in the exposed seabed, rather than on restoring the South Sea.
